text:
Oh, good God, if only you knew how I have loved you,
Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has stood
in my way, first and foremost my own nature.
Papa was likewise so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter.
But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I am
writing to you once more and telling you. I ask myself why I do
it, since after all it is a matter of indifference to you, especially
when I shall no longer even be alive; but I would like to be near
you until the end, so that at least I would not feel more
forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though
I see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements
with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then
we are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for you; I have
no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for you two days ago,
but I preferred to write. I would also prefer you to remember me
as I once was, when I had not yet been ill. I remember
that you .... (Some words have been omitted here) .... my eyes and
eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were. For that
reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I will also ask
you not to look at me in my coffin. I shall no doubt look much as
I did when I was alive, only somewhat paler, and I shall be lying
in a yellow dress; but even so, you would regret it if you came
and saw me.

Now I have returned to writing this letter many times today, and
yet I have not managed to tell you one thousandth of what I
wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to;
I still hope so fervently in God that I might perhaps
get a little better, even if only until spring. Then the days are
bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now,
I would certainly never be cruel to you again, Johannes.
How I have wept and thought of it! Oh, I would go out and pat
all the paving stones and stop and thank every step of every
staircase I passed, and be good to everyone. It would not matter
how badly I suffered, if only I were allowed to live. I would
never complain about anything again; no, I would smile at anyone
who attacked and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were
allowed to live. My life is so unlived; I have done nothing for
anyone, and this failed life is to end now. If you knew how
reluctant I am to die, then perhaps you would do something, do
everything in your power. You probably cannot do anything; but
I thought that if you and the whole world prayed for me and
would not let me go, then God would grant me life. Oh, how
grateful I would be then, and never do wrong to anyone again,
but smile at everything that befell me, if only I were allowed
to live.

Mama is sitting here weeping. She sat here all last night as well
and wept for me. This does me a little good; it softens the
bitterness of my farewell. Today I also thought: how would you
like it if I came straight up to you in the street one day, when I
was nicely dressed, and no longer said anything hurtful, but gave
you a rose that I could have bought beforehand? Then I thought
immediately afterward that I can never again do what I want;
for I can surely never recover again before I die. I weep so
often; I lie quietly and weep ceaselessly and inconsolably; my
chest does not hurt when I do not sob. Johannes, dear, dear
friend, my only beloved on earth, come to me now and stay here
for a little while when it begins to grow dark. I shall not weep
then, but smile as well as I am able, simply for joy that you came.

No, what has become of my pride and my courage! I am not my
father’s daughter now; but that is because my strength has left
me. I have

suffered for a long time, Johannes, long before these last days.
When you were abroad, I suffered, and since I came here to town
this spring, I have done nothing but suffer every day. Never
before have I known how infinitely long the night could be. I
have seen you twice in the street during this time; on one of
those occasions you were humming as you walked past me, but
you did not see me. I had hoped to see you at the Seiers’; but
you did not come. I would not have spoken to you or walked
straight in front of you, but would have been grateful merely to
see you from far away. But you did not come. I thought then that
perhaps it was because of me that you did not come. At eleven
o’clock I began to dance because I could not bear to wait any
longer. Yes, Johannes, I have loved you, loved only you throughout
my entire life. It is Victoria who is writing this, and God is
reading it over my shoulder.
And now I must bid you farewell; it has now grown almost dark,
and I can no longer see. Farewell, Johannes; thank you for every
day. When I fly away from the earth, I shall continue to thank
you until the very end and repeat your name to myself all the
way. May you fare well, then, all your life, and forgive me for
what I have done against you, and because I could not throw
myself down before you and ask your forgiveness for it. I am
doing so now in my heart. May you fare well, Johannes, and
farewell forever. And thank you once again for every single day
and hour. I can do no more.
Yours,
VICTORIA.

Now I have had the lamp lit, and it is much brighter for me.
I have lain in a stupor and once again been far away from the
earth. Thank God, it was not as frightening for me as before; I
even heard a little music, and above all, it was not dark. I am so
grateful. But now I have no strength left to write.
Farewell, my beloved ....
